families.title: Frozen fruit and vegetables
families.decision: Organic frozen produce with nothing else on the ingredient list, frozen loose.
families.why: Plain frozen fruit and vegetables are frozen piece by piece soon after harvest. A bag that has frozen into one block has likely thawed and refrozen on the way, and packs at the back of the case see the least temperature swing.
buying_tips: Look for the USDA Organic seal on the bag or box.
Read the list for the produce alone; skip citric acid, ascorbic acid and sugar.
Check the bag feels loose, pieces moving, not one solid block.
Pick packs from the back of the freezer shelf.

families.title: Bottled water
families.decision: Spring or mineral water bottled in glass or cans, nothing added.
families.why: Spring and mineral water are defined by an underground source; distilled and treated-tap water are defined by a treatment. Glass bottles or cans, with no sweeteners or flavorings, are the traditional pick.
buying_tips: Read the name: spring or mineral water comes from an underground source.
Check for “distilled” or “municipal source” wording; it names a treatment, not a spring.
Pick glass bottles or cans over plastic bottles.
Skip waters with added sweeteners or flavorings.
Look for organic certification on the chilled pack.
Read the flour line for whole grain or sprouted whole grain.
Look for pasture-raised eggs in the ingredient or sourcing statement.
Check the sealed pack's use-by date and keep-refrigerated instructions.

families.why: Miso, tempeh and natto use different cultures and recipes. Fermentation does not establish ready-to-eat status, and pasteurization does not erase fermentation. Prefer a label with useful origin and batch details.

coffee_beans.decision: Organic whole-bean coffee with a printed roast date.
coffee_beans.short_answer: Coffee is an occasional item. Pick organic whole beans in a sealed bag, and read the roast date first. Ground coffee loses flavor faster than whole beans, and open bins expose beans to air and light.
pick_steps: Read the bag for a printed roast date; skip bags without one.
Pick a sealed bag with an organic seal over open bins.

tea.decision: Organic loose-leaf herbal tea, no added flavors listed.

fermented.decision: Organic raw vegetable ferments in glass, from the cold case.

deli.decision: Organic pasture-raised whole-muscle deli meat, sliced at the counter.

frozen.short_answer: Most frozen fruit and vegetables are frozen piece by piece, quickly. A plain bag lists the produce alone. A bag frozen into one solid block has likely thawed and refrozen. Packs at the back of the shelf thaw least.
pick_steps: Shake the bag: pieces should move freely, not sit in one block.
Read the list for the fruit or vegetable alone.
Pick packs from the back of the freezer shelf.

label_natural.decision: USDA Organic seal over a bare “natural” claim.

label_organic_scope.decision: 100% organic or USDA Organic, plus a Real Organic seal.
buying_tips: The seal covers inputs and practices, and an organic cookie is still a cookie.
Organic is about inputs and practices. Read the ingredient panel separately.
Organic is the floor. Real Organic Project or Certified Naturally Grown sits above it.
A short list of approved sprays is permitted under the organic standard.
It carries the most weight on thin-skinned produce you eat whole, and the least on processed food.
On animal products it does reach feed. It means organic feed, not a different kind of feed.
Real Organic Project on top of the USDA seal means soil-grown, never hydroponic.

label_front_vs_back.decision: USDA Organic with a short whole-food ingredient list.
